clinicalPearls: Growth hormone excess arising before fusion of the epiphyseal growth plates, producing excessive linear growth and very tall stature, in contrast to acromegaly which occurs after fusion
Usually caused by a growth-hormone-secreting pituitary somatotroph adenoma, often a macroadenoma at diagnosis in children

Frequently associated with genetic or syndromic conditions including X-linked acrogigantism (GPR101 duplication), AIP mutations in familial isolated pituitary adenoma, McCune-Albright syndrome (GNAS mosaicism), Carney complex and MEN1
Acromegalic features such as coarse facies, large hands and feet and prognathism coexist with the tall stature
Growth hormone excess also causes soft-tissue overgrowth, sweating, headaches and glucose intolerance, and mass effect may cause visual disturbance and hypopituitarism
Diagnosis rests on an elevated IGF-1 for age and failure of growth hormone to suppress during an oral glucose tolerance test, together with pituitary MRI
Management combines transsphenoidal surgery with medical therapy using somatostatin analogues and the growth-hormone-receptor antagonist pegvisomant, and radiotherapy for residual disease
Screening for associated syndromes and genetic testing is important, especially in young patients
reference.pathophysiology: Pituitary gigantism results from sustained growth hormone hypersecretion, almost always from a somatotroph pituitary adenoma, occurring while the epiphyseal growth plates are still open. Growth hormone stimulates hepatic and local production of insulin-like growth factor 1, which drives chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plates and accelerated linear growth, giving excessive height, while simultaneous periosteal and soft-tissue growth produces acromegalic features. A substantial proportion of paediatric cases are genetically determined, through germline or mosaic activation of growth-promoting pathways as in X-linked acrogigantism, AIP-related familial pituitary adenomas, McCune-Albright syndrome with activating GNAS mutations, Carney complex and MEN1, and these often produce larger, earlier and more aggressive tumours than sporadic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Marfan syndrome and other connective tissue disorders
Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism) and other overgrowth syndromes
Precocious puberty with early growth acceleration then early fusion
Ectopic growth-hormone-releasing hormone secretion, which is rare
additionalInvestigations: Serum IGF-1 interpreted against age- and sex-specific reference ranges
Oral glucose tolerance test with growth hormone measurement, showing failure of growth hormone to suppress
Pituitary MRI to define the somatotroph adenoma and any invasion
Assessment of the other pituitary axes and prolactin, as co-secretion is common
Formal visual field testing if there is suprasellar extension
Genetic testing for GPR101, AIP, GNAS, MEN1 and PRKAR1A with screening for associated syndromic features
redFlags: Rapidly accelerating growth crossing height centiles in a child
Visual field loss or headache from a large invasive adenoma
Features of McCune-Albright syndrome such as cafe-au-lait patches and fibrous dysplasia, or of Carney complex, prompting syndrome workup
Cardiovascular or metabolic complications of growth hormone excess
reference.prognosis: Control can be difficult because these tumours are often large and aggressive, especially in the genetic forms, and frequently require multimodal therapy; with biochemical control final height and complications are limited, but incomplete control risks continued growth and cardiovascular and metabolic morbidity.
pitfalls: Attributing extreme tall stature to familial tall stature without measuring IGF-1
Failing to test for an underlying genetic syndrome in a young patient with gigantism
Overlooking prolactin co-secretion or other pituitary hormone deficits
Underestimating the aggressiveness and treatment resistance of syndromic somatotroph tumours
references: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Acromegaly
management: Transsphenoidal surgical resection of the somatotroph adenoma as first-line definitive treatment
Somatostatin receptor ligands such as octreotide or lanreotide to suppress growth hormone when surgery is incomplete
Growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant, alone or in combination, for persistent IGF-1 elevation
Adjunctive dopamine agonist cabergoline, particularly where prolactin is co-secreted
Radiotherapy for residual or aggressive tumour not controlled medically
Replacement of deficient anterior pituitary hormones and management of glucose intolerance
Serial IGF-1, growth velocity, visual field and metabolic surveillance
Genetic testing for AIP, GPR101, GNAS, MEN1 and PRKAR1A with counselling and family screening
